26478: Paul warns Timothy that Alexander the coppersmith did him great harm and strongly opposed his message, and says the Lord will repay him.
26479: Handed over to Satan (if the same man)
26480: 1 Timothy names an Alexander who, with Hymenaeus, had shipwrecked his faith and was put out of the church so that he might learn not to blaspheme.
26481: Alexander the coppersmith, or metalworker, is named in 2 Timothy as someone who did Paul great harm and fiercely opposed the gospel message. Timothy is told to beware of him. He may be the same Alexander who is disciplined with Hymenaeus in 1 Timothy, and some have linked him to the Alexander pushed forward in the Ephesus riot, but both identifications are uncertain.
26482: Paul leaves his judgement to the Lord: 'the Lord will repay him according to his deeds' (2 Tim 4:14). He does not say what the harm was.
26484: Alexander was a very common name. Some identify the coppersmith with the Alexander of 1 Tim 1:20 (both linked to Ephesus); fewer link him with the Jewish Alexander of the riot (Acts 19:33-34). Many scholars keep all three separate.
26486: Some think he testified against Paul at his trial, perhaps causing his final arrest; this is a guess from the legal setting of 2 Tim 4:16.
26487: Bitter and combative, a tradesman who turned his hammer against the man he once heard.
26489: Belonging to Hymen (Greek god of weddings)
26490: false teacher in the church at Ephesus
26492: Paul says Hymenaeus and Alexander rejected a good conscience and made shipwreck of their faith; he 'handed them over to Satan' so they might learn not to blaspheme.
26493: Teaches that the resurrection is past
26494: With Philetus, Hymenaeus was saying the resurrection had already happened, and their talk was spreading like gangrene and upsetting some people's faith.
26495: Hymenaeus was a teacher in the church at Ephesus whom Paul names twice as having wandered from the truth. He taught that the resurrection had already happened, probably meaning it was only a spiritual event, and Paul put him out of the fellowship so that he might be corrected. He is an example of the false teaching the Pastoral Letters warn about.
26496: 'Handing over to Satan' (1 Tim 1:20; compare 1 Cor 5:5) means excluding someone from the church. Paul states its aim as learning and correction, not destruction.
26498: Most think he taught a spiritualised resurrection, perhaps reading baptism as already raising believers fully, a view later found in some Gnostic writings. Others see an over-realised enthusiasm rather than full Gnosticism.
26499: Clever and confident, sure he has moved beyond the simple teaching of others.
26504: Greeted with the church in her house
26505: Paul sends greetings to the brothers in Laodicea and to Nympha and the church in her house.
26506: Nympha was a believer, probably in or near Laodicea, who hosted a church in her home. She is one of several women in Paul's letters who opened their houses for Christian gatherings. Some later manuscripts turned the name into the male Nymphas, but most modern translations read Nympha, a woman.
26507: Manuscripts differ between 'her house', 'his house' and 'their house' in Col 4:15; the best-supported reading is usually taken to be 'her house'.
26508: Hospitable and capable, a householder used to organising meals and meetings.
26510: Green shoot (a title of the goddess Demeter)
26511: head of a household whose people reported to Paul
26513: Paul writes that 'Chloe's people' had told him there were quarrels among the Corinthian believers.
26514: Chloe was a woman whose household members, probably servants or business agents, brought Paul news in Ephesus about divisions in the church at Corinth. Her name appears once, but her people's report helped prompt 1 Corinthians.
26515: Paul does not say whether Chloe herself was a believer, or whether she lived in Corinth or Ephesus (1 Cor 1:11).
26516: Businesslike and concerned, a woman with interests in more than one city.
26519: first convert in Achaia (with his household)
26520: leader in the church at Corinth
26522: Paul recalls that he also baptized the household of Stephanas.
26524: Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus came to Paul and refreshed his spirit. Paul calls his household the first converts of Achaia, devoted to serving the saints, and asks the church to submit to such people.
26525: Stephanas and his household were the first people in Achaia (southern Greece) to become Christians, and Paul baptized them himself. He devoted himself to serving other believers and travelled to Paul in Ephesus with two companions, probably bringing the Corinthians' letter. Paul urges the church to follow the lead of people like him.
26526: Paul calls the household the 'firstfruits of Achaia' (1 Cor 16:15), even though Acts mentions converts at Athens earlier (Acts 17:34); Paul may be thinking of Corinth's region or of the first household conversion.
26528: The baptism of 'the household of Stephanas' is often cited in debates over infant baptism; one side sees children included, the other notes the household is also said to have devoted itself to service (1 Cor 16:15).
26529: Dutiful and humble, a man who would rather carry a letter than lead a debate.
26535: Paul pleads with Euodia and Syntyche to agree in the Lord, and asks a trusted companion to help these women who had struggled beside him in the gospel.
26536: Euodia was a woman in the church at Philippi who had worked side by side with Paul in spreading the gospel. Paul publicly urges her and Syntyche to settle their disagreement and be of the same mind in the Lord. The fact that their quarrel mattered to the whole church suggests both were leaders.
26537: Paul names them with respect, as people who 'laboured side by side' with him and whose names are in the book of life (Phil 4:3). He does not say what they disagreed about.
26538: Forthright and energetic, a seasoned worker with firm opinions.
26542: Paul asks Syntyche and Euodia to agree in the Lord and asks his 'true companion' to help them, since they had contended for the gospel alongside him.
26543: Syntyche was a woman in the church at Philippi who had shared in Paul's gospel work. Paul appeals to her and Euodia to resolve their disagreement and asks a trusted colleague to help them. Paul's tone is pastoral, not harsh, and he counts both among his fellow workers.
26544: Paul repeats 'I urge' separately to each woman (Phil 4:2), treating them evenly and refusing to take sides.
26545: Thoughtful and principled, slow to back down when she believes she is right.
26550: Paul mentions Clement with the rest of his fellow workers 'whose names are in the book of life'.
26551: Clement was one of Paul's fellow workers in the church at Philippi, mentioned once in passing. Early Christian writers identified him with Clement, the later leader of the church in Rome and author of the letter known as 1 Clement, but most modern scholars think this is unlikely since Clement was a common name.
26552: Scripture says only that he worked with Paul and that his name is in the book of life (Phil 4:3).
26553: Origen and Eusebius identify this Clement with Clement of Rome, the third bishop of Rome after Peter and author of 1 Clement.
26554: Eusebius, Church History 3.4.9; Origen, Commentary on John 6.36 (needs verification)
26555: Even-tempered and gracious, a peacemaker by instinct.
26561: host to Paul and his companions
26563: Disciples from Caesarea brought Paul and his companions to stay with Mnason of Cyprus, 'an early disciple'.
26564: Mnason was a believer from Cyprus who had been a disciple from early days. On Paul's final journey to Jerusalem, Paul and his mixed Jewish and Gentile companions lodged in his home. A Cypriot Jewish believer was a natural host for a group that included Gentiles.
26565: The Greek of Acts 21:16 can mean they stayed with him in Jerusalem or in a village on the way from Caesarea; translations differ.
26566: A hospitable veteran believer who remembers the church's first days and likes to tell of them.
26569: Some date the visit to Philippi to AD 50
26570: Roman colony of Philippi (probably a Gentile)
26574: After Paul and Silas were beaten, the jailer was ordered to guard them securely, so he put them in the inner prison with their feet in stocks.
26576: At midnight, as Paul and Silas sang hymns, an earthquake opened the doors. Thinking the prisoners had escaped, the jailer drew his sword to kill himself, but Paul shouted that they were all still there.
26578: Trembling, he asked, 'What must I do to be saved?' They told him to believe in the Lord Jesus. He washed their wounds, was baptized with his household that night, and fed them, rejoicing.
26579: The jailer at Philippi was put in charge of Paul and Silas after they were beaten and thrown into prison. When an earthquake broke open the cells at midnight, he was about to kill himself, expecting to be blamed for escaped prisoners, but Paul stopped him. He asked what he must do to be saved, believed, washed the missionaries' wounds and was baptized with his household that same night.
26580: His question and Paul's answer, 'Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household' (Acts 16:30-31), are among the most quoted lines in Acts. Luke adds that they spoke the word to all in his house and that the whole household believed (Acts 16:32-34).
26581: Those who baptize infants see households like his as likely including children; believer-baptism traditions point out that the whole household also heard the word and believed (Acts 16:32-34).
26583: A guard who lost prisoners could face the penalty they would have faced (compare Acts 12:19), which explains his despair.
26584: Gruff and practical at first, then shaken and humble; a working man who knows what failure would cost him.
26588: father of seven sons who tried exorcism
26589: His sons are overpowered by a demon
26590: Seven sons of Sceva tried to drive out evil spirits by 'the Jesus whom Paul preaches'. The spirit answered that it knew Jesus and Paul but not them, and the possessed man overpowered them so that they fled naked and wounded.
26591: Sceva is described in Acts as a Jewish chief priest in Ephesus whose seven sons worked as travelling exorcists. When they tried to use the name of Jesus like a magic formula, the evil spirit turned on them and the possessed man beat them badly. The event led many in Ephesus to give up magic and burn their spell books.
26592: Acts uses the word 'chief priest' (Acts 19:14), but no high priest named Sceva is known. The burning of magic books worth fifty thousand pieces of silver follows (Acts 19:18-20).
26593: Was he really a chief priest?
26594: Many think Sceva belonged to a high-priestly family or claimed the title to impress clients; others suggest Luke reports the title the family used for itself.
26596: Usually read as showing that Jesus' name is not a spell to be borrowed but works through real relationship with him.
26597: Pompous and image-conscious, proud of a grand title he cannot quite prove.
26599: From the Roman family name Claudius, traditionally 'lame'
26605: After the murder of Caligula, the Praetorian Guard proclaimed Claudius emperor. Herod Agrippa I helped secure his accession and was rewarded with rule over Judea (Josephus). Acts mentions Claudius by name only in passing.
26606: Great famine 'in the days of Claudius'
26607: The prophet Agabus predicted a severe famine over the whole world, and Luke notes that it happened under Claudius. The church at Antioch sent relief to Judea by Barnabas and Saul.
26609: Paul met Aquila and Priscilla in Corinth because Claudius had ordered all Jews to leave Rome.
26611: A letter of Claudius inscribed at Delphi names Gallio as proconsul of Achaia, giving a fixed point for Paul's time in Corinth.
26612: Claudius was Roman emperor from AD 41 to 54, the years of much of Paul's missionary work. Acts mentions him twice: a famine in his reign prompted a relief gift from Antioch to Judea, and his order expelling Jews from Rome brought Priscilla and Aquila to Corinth, where they met Paul. Outside the Bible, the Roman historian Suetonius says the expulsion followed riots 'at the instigation of Chrestus', which many scholars think is a garbled reference to disputes about Christ.
26613: Acts names Claudius only in Acts 11:28 and Acts 18:2. The 'Caesar' of Acts 17:7 is probably Claudius too.
26615: Many scholars read Suetonius' 'Chrestus' as Christus, meaning arguments in Rome's synagogues over Jesus as Messiah. Others think Chrestus was an unknown local agitator. The date of AD 49 rests on the 5th-century writer Orosius and is also debated; some prefer AD 41.
26617: There was no single empire-wide famine, but Roman and Jewish sources record a series of serious food shortages under Claudius, including in Judea around AD 46–48.
26618: Suetonius says Claudius expelled from Rome the Jews who were constantly rioting at the instigation of Chrestus.
26620: Orosius dates the expulsion to Claudius' ninth year (AD 49), citing Josephus, though no such passage exists in our Josephus.
26622: Josephus describes famine in Judea under Claudius and relief brought by Queen Helena of Adiabene.
26624: Scholarly and pedantic, fond of history and antiquarian detail, with a halting manner that hides a sharp, administrative mind.
26631: Facing a trial in Jerusalem, Paul used his right as a Roman citizen to appeal to Caesar, that is, to Nero. Festus replied, 'To Caesar you shall go.'
26633: Festus calls the emperor 'the Augustus' (his imperial title), and an angel tells Paul in the storm that he must stand before Caesar.
26635: Paul sends greetings from saints of Caesar's household, meaning slaves or freedmen in imperial service, not necessarily Nero's family.
26637: After much of Rome burned, Nero blamed the Christians and had many put to death cruelly, according to Tacitus. This is the first known state persecution of Christians. Some scholars think the 'fiery trial' of 1 Peter reflects this setting; others date 1 Peter later.
26638: Declared a public enemy by the Senate, Nero took his own life, ending the Julio-Claudian dynasty. Rumours that he would return led some interpreters to connect him with the beast whose deadly wound was healed.
26639: Nero was Roman emperor from AD 54 to 68. He is never named in the New Testament, but he is the 'Caesar' to whom Paul appealed, and Paul wrote Romans, with its call to respect governing authorities, early in his reign. After the Great Fire of Rome in AD 64, Nero blamed and brutally executed Christians, and early church tradition holds that both Peter and Paul were martyred under him. Many scholars think the number 666 in Revelation points to him, though this is debated.
26640: Acts refers to him as 'Caesar' and 'the Augustus' (Acts 25:11-12; Acts 25:21). Romans 13 and 1 Peter 2 urge Christians to honour the emperor (Rom 13:1-7; 1 Pet 2:13-17), and were written under Nero, probably before the persecution.
26642: Many scholars note that 'Nero Caesar' written in Hebrew letters adds up to 666 (and a variant spelling to 616, a reading found in some manuscripts of Rev 13:18). Some see Nero as the beast, or as a model for it, and link the wounded-and-healed head (Rev 13:3) to rumours that Nero would return. Others, especially futurist readers, see a figure still to come; idealist readers see a symbol of all persecuting power.
26644: Some date Revelation to Nero's reign (before AD 70); most scholars prefer the reign of Domitian (c. AD 95), following Irenaeus.
26645: Tacitus says Nero blamed the fire on Christians, whom he describes as hated for their 'abominations', and had them torn by dogs, crucified, or burned as torches.
26647: Suetonius lists punishments inflicted on Christians, 'a new and harmful superstition', among Nero's measures.
26649: Peter was crucified and Paul beheaded at Rome under Nero.
26651: Vain and theatrical, craving applause as a poet and performer, with flashes of suspicion and cruelty.
26658: Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish, and sent for Paul to hear him speak about faith in Christ. When Paul spoke about justice, self-control and the coming judgement, Felix became afraid and sent him away.
26659: Drusilla was the youngest daughter of King Herod Agrippa I and sister of Agrippa II and Bernice. According to Josephus she left her first husband, the king of Emesa, to marry the Roman governor Felix. Acts says she sat with Felix as Paul spoke to them about faith, justice, self-control and judgement.
26660: Acts calls her 'a Jewess' and names her only as Felix's wife (Acts 24:24). Paul's topics of justice and self-control (Acts 24:25) may have struck home given the couple's history.
26661: Josephus says she was six when her father died, was first married to Azizus king of Emesa, and was persuaded by Felix to leave him.
26663: Josephus mentions that her son by Felix, named Agrippa, died in the eruption of Vesuvius (AD 79); whether Drusilla also died there is unclear.
26665: Poised and guarded, a royal daughter used to the politics of marriage.
26671: companion of her brother Agrippa II
26672: Arrives with Agrippa to greet Festus
26673: King Agrippa and Bernice came to Caesarea to welcome the new governor Festus.
26675: Agrippa and Bernice entered the audience hall with great pomp, with commanders and leading men of the city, to hear Paul.
26677: After Paul spoke, the king, the governor and Bernice withdrew and agreed that he had done nothing deserving death or prison.
26678: Bernice was the eldest daughter of Herod Agrippa I and sister of Agrippa II and Drusilla. Acts shows her sitting beside her brother in royal splendour when Paul made his defence at Caesarea, and joining in the verdict that Paul was innocent. Outside the Bible she had a dramatic life: married to her uncle, later to a king of Cilicia, rumoured to be too close to her brother, and later the lover of the Roman general and future emperor Titus.
26679: Acts mentions her three times, always beside Agrippa (Acts 25:13; Acts 25:23; Acts 26:30). It records no words of hers.
26681: Ancient gossip about her and her brother (Josephus, Juvenal) may reflect hostility to the Herods; modern historians treat the rumours with caution.
26682: Josephus says she was sixteen when her father died (AD 44), had married her uncle Herod of Chalcis, and later married Polemo king of Cilicia; he reports rumours about her and Agrippa.
26684: In AD 66 she stood barefoot before the governor Florus pleading for the people of Jerusalem.
26686: Roman historians say Titus loved her and that she lived with him in Rome, but he sent her away because Romans disapproved.
26687: Tacitus, Histories 2.2; Suetonius, Life of Titus 7.1
26688: Regal and self-possessed, practised at public ceremony, with a politician's caution behind her composure.
26692: Tertullus opened with lavish flattery of Felix, then accused Paul of being a plague, a stirrer of riots among Jews throughout the world, a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes, and a would-be temple defiler.
26693: Tertullus was a professional speaker hired by the high priest Ananias and the Jewish elders to present their case against Paul before the governor Felix in Caesarea. His speech begins with heavy flattery and then accuses Paul of stirring up unrest and trying to profane the temple. Paul answered each charge, and Felix postponed the case.
26694: Acts records a compressed version of his speech (Acts 24:2-8). It contains the only New Testament use of 'the sect of the Nazarenes' for Christians (Acts 24:5).
26696: His Latin name suggests he may have been a Roman or a Hellenised Jew trained in Roman legal rhetoric; Acts does not say.
26697: Polished and oily, full of compliments for the powerful and contempt for the accused.
26699: From the Roman family name Julius
26702: Paul's guard on the voyage to Rome
26705: Julius, a centurion of the Augustan Cohort, was put in charge of Paul and other prisoners. At Sidon he treated Paul kindly and let him visit friends to be cared for.
26707: Paul advised wintering at Fair Havens, but the centurion trusted the pilot and the ship's owner instead, and they sailed into the storm.
26708: Saves Paul's life in the shipwreck
26709: When the soldiers planned to kill the prisoners to stop them escaping, Julius, wanting to save Paul, stopped them and ordered everyone to swim or float to land.
26710: Receives Paul and other prisoners for the voyage to Italy.
26712: Chooses to sail on despite Paul's warning.
26713: Shipwrecked; spares the prisoners for Paul's sake.
26715: Julius was the Roman centurion, an officer over about eighty soldiers, who escorted Paul and other prisoners from Caesarea to Rome. He treated Paul kindly from the start, at first ignored his advice about the dangerous season, but later came to trust him during the storm. When his soldiers wanted to kill the prisoners as the ship broke up, Julius stopped them to save Paul's life.
26716: Acts shows his growing respect for Paul: he trusts the experts over Paul at first (Acts 27:11), but by the end acts on Paul's warnings (Acts 27:31-32) and protects him (Acts 27:43).
26718: An auxiliary unit with this title is attested in Syria and Judea; some think Julius belonged to a corps of officers who escorted prisoners and carried messages between the provinces and Rome.
26719: Disciplined and fair-minded, a professional soldier who respects courage when he sees it.
26724: Hosts the shipwrecked party and his father is healed
26725: Publius welcomed Paul and others and entertained them for three days. His father lay sick with fever and dysentery; Paul prayed, laid hands on him and healed him. Others on the island came and were healed, and the islanders honoured the travellers and supplied their needs.
26726: Publius was the leading official of Malta when Paul's ship was wrecked there. He welcomed the survivors into his home for three days. Paul prayed for Publius' sick father, who was healed, and many other islanders then came for healing.
26727: Luke calls him 'the chief man of the island' (Acts 28:7), using a title that also appears in inscriptions from Malta, which supports the accuracy of the detail.
26728: Maltese tradition holds that Publius became the first bishop of Malta and later bishop of Athens, dying as a martyr.
26729: Maltese church tradition; later Greek martyrologies (needs verification)
26730: Courteous and generous, a provincial dignitary proud of his island's hospitality.
26732: exalted people (or: the kinsman is exalted)
26734: father of Moses, Aaron and Miriam
26735: Marries Jochebed; father of Aaron and Moses
26736: Amram, son of Kohath son of Levi, marries his father's sister Jochebed, who bears Aaron, Moses and Miriam. He is said to have lived 137 years.
